scope.scopeNotesMd: This report compares the base `Signature` datatype StructureDefinition in R4 4.0.1 with the same canonical `Signature` StructureDefinition in R6 6.0.0-ballot4. Findings are limited to local `Signature` element changes. Inherited changes from `Element`, `DataType`, `Extension`, or referenced resources are called out as out of scope rather than duplicated as `Signature` findings.
outOfScope: The R6 base-definition shift from `Element` to `DataType` is a class-hierarchy/infrastructure change and is excluded under the inherited/base-artifact rule.
Inherited `Signature.id` and `Signature.extension` behavior, including the usage-site packaging of Extension constraints such as `ext-1`, belongs to the Element/Extension/DataType analyses.
Breaking changes inside reference target resources for `Signature.who` and `Signature.onBehalfOf` are owned by those resource reports.
Search parameters such as `Provenance-signature-type` and resources that contain `Signature` elements are outside this datatype-scoped report.
FHIR validator implementation behavior and external terminology server expansion behavior were not exhaustively tested.

narrativeReportMd:
# Signature R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No local hard R4→R6 instance-breaking change was found for `Signature`; the main local issue is the reverse-direction and runtime impact of R6 making `type`, `when`, and `who` optional. R4-valid signatures already contain those elements, so they remain structurally acceptable in R6, but R6-valid signatures can now omit purpose, signing time, or signer identity and therefore cannot be represented as valid R4 `Signature` instances without enrichment or extensions.

## Scope
The analysis used the R4 and R6 core `StructureDefinition-Signature.json` files, package metadata/indexes, and related local signature/mimetype terminology artifacts. Base `Element`/`DataType` inheritance changes are not reported as local findings.

## Main migration themes
R4→R6 data migration is mostly permissive: required metadata became optional, no local element was removed or renamed, and reference target lists stayed the same. Runtime consumers, validators, code generators, and business rules need updates because R6 model classes and validators must tolerate absent `type`, `when`, and `who`. R6→R4 conversion needs a policy for missing metadata: derive it, reject the record, or carry non-R4-compatible information in extensions with loss of base conformance.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact local findings are the three cardinality relaxations on `Signature.type`, `Signature.when`, and `Signature.who`. They are not hard forward validation breaks, but they are high for reverse validation and can be high in signature workflows where accountability, time of signing, or signer identity is assumed present.

## Findings requiring human review
The computable deltas are direct and high confidence. Human review is still recommended because the supplied inputs do not include the ballot rationale for relaxing all three previously mandatory accountability fields.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The change is backward compatible for existing R4 instances but not for strict R4 consumers of R6 content. A less disruptive cross-version approach would have kept the base elements required and introduced profiles or extensions for special cases, but that would have prevented the R6 base datatype from representing intentionally partial or externally carried signature metadata.

## Follow-up analysis
Review the `DataType`, `Element`, and `Extension` reports for inherited hierarchy and extension-validation behavior, and review signature terminology if enum-like code generation or terminology-driven business rules are used.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `Signature` has no local hard R4→R6 instance break. The top migration concern is that R6 permits signatures without `type`, `when`, or `who`, creating R6→R4 representability failures and runtime/nullability risk for code that assumed R4's required signature purpose, time, and signer identity. The main uncertainty is the absence of official rationale for the cardinality relaxations.
summary.migrationThemesMd: R4 data should migrate structurally because the previously required metadata is still allowed in R6. R6 consumers and generated models must treat `Signature.type`, `Signature.when`, and `Signature.who` as optional. R6→R4 transforms need enrichment or rejection rules for signatures missing any of those fields, and business logic should distinguish a structurally valid R6 signature from a locally acceptable accountable signature.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for the local StructureDefinition comparison: the same canonical StructureDefinition exists in both packages and the relevant snapshot/differential cardinality changes are explicit. Confidence is medium for semantic intent and prevalence because no official diff, Jira rationale, or rendered migration note was supplied. Terminology confidence is adequate for structural conclusions because local ValueSet compose definitions and code systems were compared, but no live expansions were run.

findings.title: Signature.type is no longer required

binding.description: An indication of the reason that an entity signed the object.

semanticText.short: Indication of the reason the entity signed the object(s)
semanticText.definition: An indication of the reason that the entity signed this document. This may be explicitly included as part of the signature information and can be used when determining accountability for various actions concerning the document.
semanticText.comment: Examples include attesting to: authorship, correct transcription, and witness of specific event. Also known as a "Commitment Type Indication".

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4 every valid `Signature` had at least one purpose/reason coding.

binding.description: An indication of the reason that an entity signed the object.

semanticText.short: Indication of the reason the entity signed the object(s)
semanticText.definition: An indication of the reason that the entity signed this document. This may be explicitly included as part of the signature information and can be used when determining accountability for various actions concerning the document.

newState.narrativeMd: In R6 a `Signature` can be structurally valid without a purpose/reason coding.

facts.note: Maximum cardinality, type, summary flag, modifier flag, and preferred binding URL are unchanged.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element keeps the same id and path, so this is a direct cardinality change rather than a rename or move.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not an R4→R6 validation break because every R4-valid instance that had `type` can still carry it in R6. It is a reverse-direction break: an R6 `Signature` without `type` is invalid against the R4 base datatype. Runtime risk is medium because generated R4-era code, FHIRPath rules, or business checks may assume the `type` array is present and non-empty when determining the accountability purpose.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Missing purpose codes can weaken audit/accountability interpretation, especially where signature type distinguishes authorship, witness, consent, validation, or timestamp signatures.

justification.inferredGoal: Permit signatures whose purpose is absent, implicit, profile-defined, or carried in the signature format rather than in the base FHIR datatype.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: lowering `Signature.type` from 1..* to 0..* preserves all R4-valid Signature instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The likely R6 goal is to avoid requiring a FHIR-level purpose code when the signature purpose is implicit, profile-defined, unavailable, or carried inside the signature format. That goal is reasonable for a permissive base datatype, and the cardinality relaxation does not invalidate R4 instances because existing `type` codings remain allowed. The change still has real R6-to-R4 and business-rule risk, so the verdict is `Probably justified` rather than fully `Justified` without ballot rationale.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Backward-compatible alternative analysis is not applicable for the R4-to-R6 base-design question: every R4-valid signature already contains `type` and remains valid after the min cardinality is lowered. Keeping `type` mandatory, using profiles, or adding conversion extensions could support stricter accountable workflows or R6-to-R4 round-tripping, but those are policy/migration mitigations and would block the R6 base goal of allowing a structurally valid signature with no separate FHIR-level purpose code.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed; the remaining tradeoff is reverse-conversion and runtime handling for R6 signatures without a purpose code.

examples.examplesMd: The first fragment is an illustrative R6 `Signature` value missing only `type`; it would fail R4 base validation because R4 requires at least one `type` coding. The migration example shows one possible enrichment when the purpose is known.

findings.narrativeMd: `Signature.type` changed from required to optional. This makes the R6 datatype more permissive, but it removes an R4 guarantee that every signature declares why the entity signed. Implementers who used this field as a mandatory accountability classifier need to update generated nullability, validation rules, and downstream business logic.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid content does not become invalid in R6 because the element is still allowed with the same type and binding. A valid R6 signature that omits `type` cannot be represented as a valid R4 `Signature` without adding a coding or using a non-base workaround. Strict R4 validators, non-empty-list assumptions, and enum-like processing over signature purpose are the main failure modes.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4→R6, preserve existing `type` values. For R6→R4, derive the purpose from local workflow, the cryptographic signature package, the containing resource, or a profile-specific rule; otherwise reject the conversion or carry an explicit data-absent-reason-like extension with the understanding that the base R4 cardinality is still not satisfied. Test missing, single, and multiple purpose codings.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is backward compatible for existing R4 instances but not for reverse conversion. The likely goal could have been broader support for signatures where purpose is implicit or external. A base-compatible alternative would have used profiles or extensions for such cases, trading interoperability guarantees for flexibility.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review should confirm whether R6 intentionally permits purpose-less signatures in the base datatype or expects profiles to re-require this element for accountable workflows.

findings.title: Signature.when is no longer required

semanticText.definition: When the digital signature was signed.
semanticText.comment: This should agree with the information in the signature.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4 every valid `Signature` had a signing instant.

semanticText.definition: When the digital signature was signed.
semanticText.comment: This should agree with the information in the signature.

newState.narrativeMd: In R6 a `Signature` can be structurally valid without a signing instant.

facts.note: Maximum cardinality and primitive type are unchanged.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element keeps the same id and path, so this is a direct cardinality change.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is permissive for R4→R6 validation but breaking for R6→R4 validation because R4 requires a signing instant. Runtime risk is high for code generated from R4 or business rules that sort, audit, expire, or verify signatures using a non-null signing time.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Missing signing time can affect audit trails, legal defensibility, freshness checks, and signature verification workflows even when the cryptographic package may contain its own timestamp.

justification.inferredGoal: Permit signatures where the signing time is unknown, unavailable, or only available inside the signature payload.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: lowering `Signature.when` from 1..1 to 0..1 preserves all R4-valid Signature instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The likely R6 goal is to permit signatures where the signing instant is unknown, unavailable at the FHIR layer, or only present inside the cryptographic payload. That is a plausible base-model goal, and the relaxation is not a forward instance break because R4 signatures that include `when` still validate in R6. The unchanged comment that `when` should agree with signature information makes the field semantically important, so the missing official rationale prevents a stronger verdict.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Backward-compatible alternative analysis is not applicable for preserving R4 instances because the R6 cardinality widening already preserves them. Requiring `when` in profiles, extracting a timestamp during down-conversion, or carrying absent-reason information can mitigate local audit and R6-to-R4 needs, but those are not less-breaking base R6 alternatives; keeping `when` required would fail the R6 goal of allowing signatures whose time is not exposed as a FHIR `instant`.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed; R6-to-R4 conversion may need rejection or trusted timestamp extraction.

examples.examplesMd: The first fragment is validly shaped for R6 with respect to `when` but would fail R4 because `when` is absent. The migration example is only safe if the timestamp can be reliably derived.

findings.narrativeMd: `Signature.when` changed from mandatory to optional. This removes an R4 structural guarantee that a signature value exposes the signing instant in FHIR, even though the same time may exist inside a cryptographic signature container.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Existing R4 signatures with `when` remain valid in R6. R6 signatures without `when` are not valid R4 signatures. Code generated from R4 may expose `when` as non-null, and audit or verification pipelines may fail or silently assign incorrect defaults if this optionality is not handled explicitly.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Preserve R4 `when` values during forward migration. For R6→R4 conversion, extract the signing time from the signature payload only if the extraction is trusted and deterministic; otherwise reject or flag the conversion rather than fabricating a timestamp. Add tests for missing `when`, timezone/instant precision, and conflicts between FHIR-level `when` and embedded signature timestamps.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The relaxation may be justified when signature formats carry their own timestamp or when non-electronic signatures lack an exact instant. The backward-compatible alternative was to keep the base field required and represent exceptions using profiles/extensions, but that would reduce the base datatype's ability to model partial signature context.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Review whether local policy should re-require `when` even though the R6 base datatype does not.

findings.title: Signature.who is no longer required

semanticText.definition: A reference to an application-usable description of the identity that signed  (e.g. the signature used their private key).
semanticText.comment: This should agree with the information in the signature.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4 every valid `Signature` had a signer reference.

semanticText.definition: A reference to an application-usable description of the identity that signed  (e.g. the signature used their private key).
semanticText.comment: This should agree with the information in the signature.

newState.narrativeMd: In R6 a `Signature` can be structurally valid without a signer reference.

facts.note: Maximum cardinality, Reference type, and target profile list are unchanged.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element keeps the same id and path, so this is a direct cardinality change.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a forward validation break because R4 signatures with a signer reference remain valid in R6. It is a high reverse-direction and runtime risk because R6 allows a signature without a FHIR-level signer identity, while R4 validators, generated classes, authorization checks, audit displays, and non-repudiation workflows may assume `who` is present.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Missing signer identity can materially affect accountability, authorization, legal attestation, and patient-safety review of signed clinical or administrative content.

justification.inferredGoal: Permit signatures where signer identity is embedded in the cryptographic payload or not resolvable to a FHIR resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: lowering `Signature.who` from 1..1 to 0..1 preserves all R4-valid Signature instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The likely R6 goal is to support signatures whose signer identity is embedded in cryptographic material or cannot be represented as one of the allowed FHIR reference targets. That is a reasonable expressivity goal for the base datatype, and it does not invalidate R4 instances that already carry `who`. Because signer identity is central to accountability and the inspected inputs do not include the ballot rationale, the change is only probably justified and should still be profiled more strictly where legal, safety, or audit policy requires it.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: For the R4-to-R6 direction, no backward-compatible alternative is needed: R4 `who` references remain valid in R6. Adding extensions, conversion rules, or local profiles can help represent non-FHIR signer evidence or require signer identity for accountable workflows, but those are mitigations rather than less-breaking base-design alternatives. Keeping `who` mandatory would preserve R6-to-R4 round-trip behavior but would not meet the inferred R6 base goal of allowing signatures without a separate FHIR-level signer reference.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed; strict accountability workflows should profile `who` back to required rather than treating that as a base alternative.

examples.examplesMd: The first fragment is an illustrative R6 `Signature` missing only `who`; it cannot satisfy the R4 base datatype. The migration example is only lossless if a reliable signer reference can be supplied.

findings.narrativeMd: `Signature.who` changed from required to optional. This is the most operationally significant local change because signer identity is central to interpreting a signature. Systems that treat a `Signature` as proof that a known FHIR actor signed must now distinguish base R6 validity from local trust-policy validity.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 signatures with `who` remain valid in R6, but R6 signatures without `who` are invalid in R4. Generated R4-era APIs may expose `who` as required, and R6 parsers/validators must not reject absent `who` unless a profile re-requires it. Business rules must avoid treating absent `who` as an anonymous but still fully accountable signature without explicit policy.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Preserve existing signer references on forward migration. For R6→R4, map certificate subject, device identity, organization identity, or containing workflow context to one of the allowed target resource types only when that mapping is trustworthy; otherwise reject lossless conversion or use a profile-specific extension while noting that base R4 conformance is not achieved. Test omitted `who`, contained signer references, and each target profile type.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The relaxation may support signatures whose identity is embedded in non-FHIR cryptographic material or cannot be represented as a FHIR `Reference`. A less disruptive design would have added a new optional alternative for external signer identity while preserving `who`, but that would have been more complex and might still not cover every signature technology.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Local policies for legal, consent, or clinical-signature workflows should probably profile `Signature.who` back to `1..1` unless the signer identity is guaranteed elsewhere.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The canonical URL, id, name, type, kind, derivation, and abstract flag are stable. The base-definition shift to `DataType` and standards-status advancement are noted but not treated as a local breaking identity change.

No local `Signature` element was removed, renamed, split, merged, or added. The local element set remains `type`, `when`, `who`, `onBehalfOf`, `targetFormat`, `sigFormat`, and `data`, plus inherited `id` and `extension`.
All local element type codes are unchanged: `Coding`, `instant`, `Reference`, `code`, and `base64Binary` remain in the same locations.
`Signature.who` and `Signature.onBehalfOf` keep the same target profile list: Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson, Patient, Device, and Organization.

`Signature.type` remains a preferred binding to `ValueSet/signature-type`; R6 widens that value set to include ETSI codes and this is recorded as a notable non-breaking change. `targetFormat` and `sigFormat` remain required bindings to `ValueSet/mimetypes`; the value set version changes from `4.0.1` to `6.0.0-ballot4`, but both local compose definitions include all codes from `urn:ietf:bcp:13`. No live expansion was run.
No local `Signature`-specific invariant was added or removed. The common `ele-1` constraint remains present. Inherited `Extension` constraint packaging is out of scope for this datatype report.
No local element became a modifier or stopped being a modifier.
`type`, `when`, `who`, and `onBehalfOf` remain summary elements; `targetFormat`, `sigFormat`, and `data` remain non-summary.
No local slicing is defined on `Signature` elements. Inherited slicing on `extension` is not a local Signature content-model change.
No local fixed value, pattern, or default value was found in either version.
No local maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue constraints were found on Signature elements.
Wire element names and primitive/complex type names are unchanged. Serialization/codegen risk comes from changed nullability of `type`, `when`, and `who`, which is covered in the findings.
The material R6→R4 representability risks are the three cardinality relaxations. No additional local element additions or type widenings create R6-only wire content.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Signature advances from draft/trial-use to active/normative metadata
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: This changes conformance metadata, not instance wire format. It does not by itself make any R4 instance invalid in R6.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Governance tooling and documentation may treat the R6 datatype as more stable. Do not infer that the base-definition shift should be handled in this local report; that is a base datatype hierarchy concern.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Preferred Signature.type value set now includes ETSI signature type codes
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `Signature.type` has a preferred binding, so instances are not required to use only the listed codes. R4 data using ASTM codes remains valid, and the R4 base datatype can still carry ETSI `Coding` values structurally even though they were not in the R4 preferred value set.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology-aware UIs, picklists, documentation, and enum-like generated helpers should add the ETSI system `http://uri.etsi.org/01903/v1.2.2` and its six local codes while preserving the existing ASTM system `urn:iso-astm:E1762-95:2013`.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Signature.data comment now explicitly mentions XML Signature and JSON Jose use
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element name, type, cardinality, and constraints are unchanged. The text appears to clarify signature technology examples and that XML Signature can be generated for a JSON resource, rather than imposing a new validation rule.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Implementers should avoid hard-coding R4-era text that assumes XML-Signature only signs XML-form resources. Signature verification libraries may need tests for the payload format indicated by `targetFormat` and the signature format indicated by `sigFormat`.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Mime Types required binding version changes to the R6 ballot value set version
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Both R4 and R6 local ValueSet definitions include all codes from `urn:ietf:bcp:13`; only the value set version and description text changed in the inspected package artifacts.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: StructureDefinition consumers should update binding URLs from `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/mimetypes|4.0.1` to `|6.0.0-ballot4`. Terminology servers may still vary in live BCP-13 expansion behavior.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: `Signature` now specializes `DataType` rather than directly specializing `Element`; this inherited class-hierarchy shift should be handled in the `DataType`/base artifact analysis.
Inherited `id`/`extension` behavior and constraint packaging are visible in the snapshot but are not local `Signature` findings.

The R6 preferred value set adds the ETSI signature type code system. A terminology-focused review could assess exact expansion, display/definition changes, and ConceptMap needs for implementations that expose signature type picklists or enums.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4→R6 diff, ballot rationale, or Jira/change note was available to explain the cardinality relaxations.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review the official Signature datatype change history, ballot issue, or migration guide for the rationale and intended profiling guidance.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Terminology conclusions are based on local ValueSet compose definitions and local CodeSystem resources; no external terminology-server expansion was run.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run version-specific terminology expansions for `ValueSet/signature-type` and `ValueSet/mimetypes` with the same terminology server used by target implementations.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The R6 input is a ballot build package (`6.0.0-ballot4`) marked not for publication in package metadata, so final R6 content may differ.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Re-run the comparison against the final published R6 core package when available.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The analysis did not execute a matrix of R4 and R6 official validators on illustrative instance fragments; compatibility mechanisms were inferred from StructureDefinition cardinalities and bindings.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Validate representative resources containing `Signature` values against both R4 and R6 definitions using target validator versions.
